Dragonfly {{i60f55b229e864}} 

A  {{i60f55b229ecc3}}is an insect belonging to the order Odonata, infraorder  {{i60f55b229ed88}}Anisoptera (from Greek ἄνισος anisos, "unequal" and πτερόν pteron, "wing", because the hindwing is broader than the forewing).{{i60f55b229eee7}} dragonflies {{i60f55b229ef9b}} are characterized by {{i60f55b229f0c0}}large, multifaceted {{i60f55b229f22a}}eyes, two pairs of strong, transparent wings, sometimes with coloured patches, and an elongated body. Dragonflies can be mistaken for the related group, damselflies (Zygoptera), which are similar in structure, though usually lighter in build; however, the wings of most dragonflies are held flat and away from the body, while  {{i60f55b229f27c}}damselflies{{i60f55b229f3a4}} hold their wings{{i60f55b229f4a4}}  folded at rest, along or above the abdomen. {{i60f55b229f68b}}Dragonflies are agile fliers, while damselflies have a weaker, fluttery flight. Many dragonflies have brilliant iridescent or  {{i60f55b229f73a}}metallic colours produced by structural colouration, making them conspicuous in flight. An adult dragonfly's compound eyes have nearly 24,000 ommatidia each.

Fossils of very large dragonfly ancestors in the Protodonata are found from 325 million {{i60f55b229f8c8}}  years{{i60f55b229fa21}} ago (Mya) in Upper Carboniferous rocks; these had wingspans up to about 750 mm (30 in). About 3,000 extant species are known. Most are tropical, with fewer species in temperate regions. Loss of wetland habitat threatens dragonfly populations around the world.

Dragonflies{{i60f55b229fb3e}}  are predators, both in their aquatic larval stage, when they are known as {{i60f55b229fe34}}nymphs or naiads, and as adults. In some species, the nymphal stage lasts for up to five years, and the adult stage may be as long as ten weeks, but most species have an adult lifespan in the order of five weeks or less, and some survive for only a few days.[2] They are fast, agile{{i60f55b229fead}}  fliers, sometimes migrating across oceans, and often live near water. They have a uniquely complex mode of reproduction involving indirect insemination, delayed fertilization, and sperm competition. During mating, the male grasps the female at the  {{i60f55b22b5de5}}back of the head, and the female curls her abdomen under her body to pick up sperm from the male's secondary genitalia at the front of his abdomen, forming the "heart" or "wheel" posture.

Dragonflies are represented in human culture on artefacts such as pottery, rock {{i60f55b22b5f0e}}paintings, statues and Art Nouveau jewellery.{{i60f55b22b604e}}  They are used in traditional medicine in Japan and China, and caught for food in Indonesia. They are symbols of courage, strength, and happiness in Japan, but seen as sinister in European folklore. Their bright colours and agile flight are{{i60f55b22b6149}}  admired in the poetry of Lord{{i60f55b22b6274}}  Tennyson and the prose of H. E. Bates.
